sections.title: Description and History
sections.summary: Opening part of Chapter 7: introduces the deep mixing and mass mixing methods, how they blend binder with soil in situ to make soil-cement, their history, the focus and scope of the chapter, a recommended glossary, and the primary references (pp. 7-1 to 7-8).
sections.body: Part 1.0 of the chapter (pp. 7-1 to 7-8) describes deep mixing and mass mixing and their history. It contains an introduction (1.1), a description, historical overview, focus and scope for each method (1.2), a glossary of recommended terminology (1.3) and the primary references (1.4).
key_points: Covers introduction, description and history, glossary and primary references for both methods.
sections.applicability: Deep mixing support of embankments, walls, abutments and other structures on soft ground in transportation projects.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Deep mixing and mass mixing blend a binder with soil in situ to produce soil-cement of higher strength and lower compressibility. Describes binders, the wet and dry methods, the types of mixing equipment, and three ways mass mixing generally differs from deep mixing (p. 7-1).
sections.body: Both the deep mixing method and the mass mixing method blend a binder with soil in situ to produce soil-cement with improved properties, such as increased strength and reduced compressibility, compared to the untreated soil. The improved ground can support embankments, retaining walls, bridge abutments and other structures. Deep mixing has also been used for seepage barriers, but because they are rarely needed in transportation projects that application is outside the chapter's scope (p. 7-1). Binders can be cement, lime, fly ash, slag or other materials, or blends; in current United States practice cement and slag-cement blends are most common. Pre-mixing the binder with water to a slurry that is mixed into the ground is the wet mixing method; delivering dry binder pneumatically is the dry mixing method. Equipment types include vertical-axis mixing equipment with blades on one or more shafts (single columns or overlapping columns from one set-up), cutter-type equipment with two wheels rotating in opposite directions about horizontal axes (rectangular elements), chainsaw-type mixers that cut continuous trenches as the track-mounted machine crawls, and horizontally rotating toothed drums on an excavator stick that treat large areas to relatively shallow depth. Binder injection ports are at or near the cutting and mixing blades or teeth. Deep mixing and mass mixing have no precise distinction. Mass mixing generally differs in three respects: (1) area coverage of 100% or nearly 100%; (2) typically lower design strength; and (3) treatment depth that may be less than in some deep mixing applications.
key_points: Soil-cement from in situ blending of binder and soil has increased strength and reduced compressibility.
Cement and slag-cement blends are the most common binders in current United States practice.
Wet method: binder-water slurry mixed into the ground; dry method: dry binder delivered pneumatically.
Equipment: vertical-axis shafts, horizontal-axis cutter wheels, chainsaw-type trenchers, and excavator-mounted toothed drums.
Mass mixing: 100% or nearly 100% coverage, typically lower design strength, and possibly shallower treatment than deep mixing.
Seepage barriers are outside the chapter's scope.

sections.title: Deep Mixing
sections.summary: Deep mixing by the wet method (all soil types incl. organic soils and peat) and the dry method (soft fine-grained and organic soils, peat); elements, development since the 1960s, U.S. use since the 1990s, and the chapter's role as an overview of FHWA (2013) (pp. 7-1 to 7-4).
sections.body: Deep mixing can be done by the wet method (Figure 7-1) or the dry method (Figure 7-2). The wet method can be used in coarse-grained, fine-grained and organic soils and peat; for transportation projects it generally uses vertical-axis single-shaft or multiple-shaft equipment, or cutter soil mixing equipment with horizontally rotating cutting and mixing wheels. The dry method can be used in soft fine-grained soils and in organic soils and peat, generally with a vertical-axis single-column tool with cutting and mixing blades near the bottom of the shaft (p. 7-3). Each machine set-up creates a vertical element: a single cylinder, a set of overlapping cylinders, or a rectangular prism of soil-cement. The treated ground is commonly called soil-cement regardless of binder. Elements can be used individually or overlapped to form walls, grids or blocks. Important development of the method occurred outside the United States from the 1960s. U.S. transportation use began in the 1990s, with more than 20 major projects to date. Before about 2010, impediments were unfamiliarity, lack of accessible analysis and design procedures, and concern about QC/QA; these changed through FHWA and Army Corps of Engineers research and technology transfer and international deep mixing conferences in 2003, 2012 and 2015. Post-hurricane levee and floodwall projects, one involving approximately 1.7 million cubic yards of in-place soil-cement, built familiarity and robust QC/QA procedures and led to the FHWA deep mixing manual published in 2013. Deep mixing is now also commonly used for remediation of dams, which share settlement and stability issues with transportation embankments. Because FHWA (2013) and the other primary references give the information needed for design and construction, the chapter is a summary and overview (pp. 7-3 to 7-4).
key_points: Wet method: coarse-grained, fine-grained and organic soils and peat; dry method: soft fine-grained soils, organic soils and peat.
An element is a single cylinder, overlapping cylinders, or a rectangular prism formed at one machine set-up.
Elements can be used individually or overlapped into walls, grids or blocks.
U.S. transportation use began in the 1990s; more than 20 major projects completed.
One levee project involved approximately 1.7 million cubic yards of in-place soil-cement.
The chapter summarizes the FHWA (2013) deep mixing manual (FHWA-HRT-13-046).

sections.title: Mass Mixing
sections.summary: Mass mixing (higher replacement ratios, shallower depth, lower strength than deep mixing) by wet or dry method: shallow soil mixing with large-diameter single-axis equipment, and mass stabilization with an excavator-mounted horizontal-axis tool to about 20 feet; combined use with deep mixing (pp. 7-4 to 7-5).
sections.body: Mass mixing generally involves higher area replacement ratios (100% or nearly 100%), shallower treatment depths and lower strengths than deep mixing, but the two are very similar without a clear distinction, so a good understanding of deep mixing is necessary background (p. 7-4). It can be done by the wet or dry method and includes shallow soil mixing and mass stabilization. Shallow soil mixing generally uses large-diameter, single-axis, vertical-shaft equipment with the wet method, and has been used in the United States for several decades to support embankments and structures and to immobilize contaminants. Mass stabilization uses an excavator-mounted, horizontal-axis mixing tool (Figure 7-3). Pioneered outside the United States in the mid-1990s, it is generally done in that practice by the dry method with binder delivered pneumatically through the tool head; in the United States both dry and wet methods have been used. It generally gives complete coverage in a series of connected, overlapping blocks and can treat soils to a depth of about 20 feet (p. 7-5). Mass mixing has been combined with deep mixing by first mass mixing a platform and then installing deep mixed elements through it, with pre-drilling sometimes needed. The platform provides a working surface and acts as a load transfer platform that reduces the number of deep mixed elements. FHWA (2013) does not explicitly address mass mixing; the chapter advises learning deep mixing first and then reading for the differences.
key_points: Mass mixing = shallow soil mixing plus mass stabilization.
Mass stabilization uses an excavator-mounted horizontal-axis tool and treats to about 20 feet.
A mass mixed platform can serve as working surface and load transfer platform for deep mixed elements installed through it.
Pre-drilling through the platform may be needed depending on its strength and the equipment power.
FHWA (2013) does not explicitly address mass mixing.

sections.title: Glossary
sections.summary: Recommended industry-wide terminology for deep and mass mixing: binder, binder content, binder factor, binder factor in-place, blade rotation number, column, element, mass mixing, soil-cement, strength, stroke, volume ratio, wall, water-to-binder ratio, wet and dry mixing (pp. 7-5 to 7-8).
sections.body: Recommended definitions (pp. 7-5 to 7-8). Binder: chemically reactive material (lime, cement, gypsum, blast furnace slag, fly ash or other hardening reagents) mixed with in situ soil to form soil-cement. Binder content: weight of dry binder to dry weight of soil treated. Binder factor: weight of dry binder to volume of soil treated. Binder factor in-place: weight of dry binder to volume of mixture (soil plus slurry for the wet method, or plus dry binder for the dry method). Blade rotation number (BRN): total mixing blade passes per meter of vertical shaft movement, for vertical-axis rotary methods; for horizontal-axis cutters, cutter wheel rotations per meter of depth may be reported. Column: pillar of treated soil from a single installation. Element: produced by one penetration and withdrawal at a single set-up; a chainsaw-type tool produces a continuous wall, not an element. Mass mixing: 100% or nearly 100% coverage, not more than about 30 feet deep, and lower strength than many deep mixing applications, with no precise dividing line. Soil-cement: mixture of in situ soil and binder. Strength: for design usually shear strength; in QC/QA usually unconfined compressive strength; always identify which. Stroke: one penetration and withdrawal cycle. Volume ratio: volume of slurry injected to volume of soil. Wall: overlapping columns or elements forming a continuous wall (shear wall or buttress, cutoff wall, excavation support wall). Water-to-binder ratio: weight of water to weight of dry binder, with slurry and total-water definitions. Also defined: restroke, retrieval, rotation speed, penetration/retrieval speed, withdrawal rate, dry and wet mixing.
key_points: Binder factor = weight of dry binder per volume of soil to be treated; binder content = dry binder weight over dry soil weight.
BRN = total number of mixing blade passes per meter of vertical shaft movement.
Mass mixing per the glossary: 100% or nearly 100% coverage, not more than about 30 feet deep.
Design 'strength' usually means shear strength; QC/QA 'strength' usually means unconfined compressive strength.
Wet mixing total-water-to-binder ratio = (slurry water + soil water) / dry binder weight.
sections.applicability: Consistent terminology in deep mixing and mass mixing design, specifications and QC/QA records.

sections.title: Applications
sections.summary: Deep mixing increases strength and decreases compressibility of soft ground under embankments, retaining walls, abutments and bridge piers, unreinforced; with steel reinforcement for excavation support. Wet method suits large projects; dry method has lower mobilization but lower strengths (p. 7-9).
sections.body: In transportation infrastructure, deep mixing can increase the strength and decrease the compressibility of soft ground supporting embankments, retaining walls, abutments, bridge piers and other structures; in these applications the soil-cement is used without reinforcement. Deep mixing can also be used for excavation support, typically with vertical steel reinforcement and lateral bracing or tie-back anchors (p. 7-9). The wet method tends to be most useful for relatively large embankment projects because of mobilization costs, and in such cases it can also be economical for foundation support of retaining walls and abutments. The dry method tends to have lower mobilization costs and may suit many projects, although design strengths for dry mixed materials are generally lower than for wet mixed materials. Wet mixing equipment is more capable than the lighter dry mixing equipment where dense and hard materials must be penetrated.
key_points: Soil-cement for embankment and structure support is used without reinforcement.
Excavation support typically uses vertical steel reinforcement with bracing or tie-backs.
Wet method: most useful for relatively large embankment projects due to mobilization cost.
Dry method: lower mobilization cost but generally lower design strengths.
Wet equipment penetrates dense and hard materials better than dry equipment.

sections.title: Advantages and Potential Disadvantages

sections.body: This section lists the advantages of deep mixing (Section 2.1.2.1) and its potential disadvantages (Section 2.1.2.2), pp. 7-9 to 7-10.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.summary: Advantages of deep mixing: strengthens soft silts, clays, organic soils and peat; faster than PVDs with preload; prevents liquefaction; penetrates dense layers; allows steeper slopes; adjustable design; protects adjacent facilities; little spoil; no dewatering; low noise (pp. 7-9 to 7-10).
sections.body: Advantages of deep mixing listed on pp. 7-9 to 7-10: it increases the strength and decreases the compressibility of soft silts, clays, organic soils and peat; improves soft clay deposits more quickly than prefabricated vertical drains with preloads and surcharging; prevents liquefaction of loose sand deposits; powerful wet-mixing equipment can penetrate dense and strong layers to treat underlying weak, loose or compressible layers; permits reduced embankment footprint and fill volume through steeper side slopes or vertical walls; the plan arrangement, treatment depth and degree of improvement can be easily adjusted to design requirements and subsurface conditions; carries new loads placed next to existing facilities so they do not settle the existing facilities; has high production capacity with large equipment; treats materials in situ, reducing disposal problems (the dry method produces very little to no spoils, and wet-method spoils make excellent fill); stabilizes many contaminants; can be used on dry land and marine projects; is economical on large projects; needs no dewatering; and produces less noise and vibration than some other technologies.
key_points: Improves soft clay faster than prefabricated vertical drains with preloading.
Prevents liquefaction of loose sand deposits.
Allows steeper side slopes or vertical walls, reducing footprint and fill volume.
Dry method produces very little to no spoils; wet-method spoils make excellent fill.
No dewatering needed; less noise and vibration than some other technologies.
sections.applicability: Deep mixing support of embankments, walls, abutments and other structures on soft ground in transportation projects.

sections.title: Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: Potential disadvantages of deep mixing: higher mobilization and unit costs than PVDs with preloading, need for specialized engineering familiarity, obstructions, buried utilities, heavy wet-method equipment on soft ground, spoils disposal, and elements not normally battered (p. 7-10).
sections.body: Potential disadvantages and limitations of deep mixing (p. 7-10): mobilization and unit costs can be higher than for other technologies such as prefabricated vertical drains with preloading; the engineer must be familiar with specialized design, construction, specification and QC/QA practices; cobbles, boulders, dense sand deposits, buried logs and other obstructions can interfere with penetration; buried utilities and structures must be avoided, and if they cannot be spanned and treatment immediately next to them is needed another technology such as jet grouting may be required; the wet method generally uses heavy equipment that can require timber mats or other techniques on soft ground; wet-method spoils may have to be hauled off site if there is no on-site use for the fill; and deep mixed elements are not normally installed at significant batters, which is generally not a limitation for highway applications where elements are almost always vertical.
key_points: Mobilization and unit costs can exceed those of prefabricated vertical drains with preloading.
Obstructions (cobbles, boulders, dense sand, buried logs) can interfere with penetration.
Jet grouting may be needed immediately next to buried utilities or structures.
Heavy wet-method equipment may need timber mats on soft ground.
Elements are not normally installed at significant batters.

sections.title: Geotechnical
sections.summary: Deep mixing is feasible in very soft to medium stiff clays, very loose to medium dense sands, very soft to medium stiff organic soils, and peat; wet equipment can penetrate stiff or dense layers, but gravels, cobbles, boulders and logs may need predrilling (p. 7-11).
sections.body: Deep mixing is a feasible ground improvement method in very soft to medium stiff clays, very loose to medium dense sands, very soft to medium stiff organic soils, and peat (p. 7-11). Powerful wet-method equipment can penetrate stiff clays and dense sands to reach underlying soft, loose and organic deposits, but dense gravels, cobbles, boulders, logs and other obstructions can make penetration difficult or impossible without predrilling or other pretreatment, which increases costs. Dry method equipment is typically lighter than wet method equipment and is not as capable of penetrating dense or hard layers.
key_points: Feasible soils: very soft to medium stiff clays and organic soils, very loose to medium dense sands, and peat.
Dense gravels, cobbles, boulders and logs may require predrilling or pretreatment.
Dry method equipment is less capable of penetrating dense or hard layers.
sections.applicability: Screening a site's soils for deep mixing feasibility.

sections.title: Environmental Considerations
sections.summary: Cement immobilizes contaminants, so deep mixing may be suitable or preferred in contaminated ground; deep mixing in freezing conditions needs insulated, heated slurry lines at added cost, and freeze-thaw damage should be considered above frost depth (p. 7-11).
sections.body: Cement is often used to treat contaminated ground in situ by immobilizing contaminants, so deep mixing may be a suitable or even preferred method for improving the mechanical behavior of contaminated ground (p. 7-11). Deep mixing has been done in freezing conditions using insulated and heated slurry delivery lines, which increases cost. The potential for freeze-thaw cycles to damage the soil-cement should be considered, but temperature fluctuations are not known to be detrimental below the frost depth.
key_points: Deep mixing can improve contaminated ground while immobilizing contaminants.
Freezing conditions require insulated, heated slurry lines.
Freeze-thaw is not known to be detrimental below frost depth.
sections.applicability: Deep mixing in contaminated ground or cold climates.

sections.title: Site Conditions
sections.summary: Site needs for deep mixing: space for an equipment yard and slurry batch plant for the wet method, little space for dry equipment, working platforms or mats on very soft ground, groundwater generally not a problem, and options for buried utilities (p. 7-11).
sections.body: For the wet method, space is needed for an equipment yard, a slurry batch plant and equipment maneuvering; comparatively little space is needed for lighter dry mixing equipment, and no slurry plant (p. 7-11). If near-surface ground is too soft to support the equipment, a working platform and/or timber mats or steel plates may be needed. High groundwater levels are not problematic except as they contribute to the need for a working platform or other equipment support. Buried utilities and structures can interfere with deep mixing; potential solutions are designing the ground improvement and overlying facilities to span the utility, relocating the utility, and using jet grouting between the deep mixing and the utility or structure.
key_points: The wet method needs space for an equipment yard, slurry batch plant and maneuvering.
High groundwater is not problematic in itself.
Buried utilities: span them, relocate them, or jet grout between them and the deep mixing.
sections.applicability: Planning site logistics for deep mixing.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.summary: Limitations of deep mixing: treatment depths typically limited to about 130 feet, and dense or hard soils, cobbles, boulders, obstructions, and buried utilities or structures can limit its application (p. 7-12).
sections.body: Limitations of deep mixing (p. 7-12): treatment depths are typically limited to about 130 feet; and dense or hard soils, cobbles, boulders, obstructions, and buried utilities or structures can limit the application of deep mixing.
key_points: Treatment depth typically limited to about 130 feet.
Dense or hard soils, cobbles, boulders, obstructions and buried utilities can limit use.

sections.title: Alternative Solutions (or Technologies)
sections.summary: Likely alternatives to deep mixing: prefabricated vertical drains with preloading and surcharging (often least expensive but slow), vibrating probe densification or deep dynamic compaction in coarse-grained soils, and piles, aggregate columns or vibro-concrete columns with column-supported embankments (p. 7-12).
sections.body: Likely alternatives to deep mixing, each to be evaluated for its ability to meet project objectives and for its own advantages, disadvantages and limitations (p. 7-12): prefabricated vertical drains with preloading and surcharging, often the least expensive option for compressible silts and clays, though it can take considerable time, settlements may continue, and new embankment placed next to existing embankment can settle the existing embankment; densification by vibrating probes or deep dynamic compaction, effective in coarse-grained soils where project conditions permit; and piles, aggregate columns or vibro-concrete columns with column-supported embankments, effective in many circumstances where deep mixing is also an option, with project size, constraints and subsurface conditions governing the choice.
key_points: Prefabricated vertical drains with preloading: often least expensive for compressible silts and clays, but slow.
Vibro densification or deep dynamic compaction for coarse-grained soils.
Column-supported embankments on piles, aggregate columns or vibro-concrete columns.
sections.applicability: Comparing deep mixing with other ground improvement options.

sections.title: Construction
sections.summary: Deep mixing methods differ by wet/dry, vertical-axis, horizontal-axis or chainsaw mixing, end or shaft binder delivery, and slurry pressure. Covers the wet-method slurry plant, heavy equipment, slurry injection during penetration with double-stroking, cutter soil mixing, and dry method practice (pp. 7-12 to 7-13).
sections.body: Mixing methods differ by: wet or dry method; vertical-axis rotary (single- and multiple-axis), horizontal-axis rotary (cutter wheel and toothed-drum) and vertical chainsaw-type mixing; end or shaft delivery of binder for vertical-axis mixing; and low, medium or high pressure slurry delivery (p. 7-12). The wet method requires a slurry plant with binder storage silos, slurry mixing equipment, agitation tank(s) and pump(s); quality control of slurry preparation and delivery keeps proportions constant. Wet equipment is typically large and heavy, so working platforms with or without timber mats may be needed, and an excavator typically supports each rig to move mats and spoils (p. 7-13). Slurry can be delivered on penetration or withdrawal. For vertical-axis mixing, U.S. practice most commonly injects slurry during penetration through nozzles near the bottom of the shaft or the bottom cutting blades, so the slurry is mixed on both downstroke and upstroke. Good practice often includes double-stroking and/or dwell time at the bottom of the element where mixing blade passes would otherwise be fewer. For wet cutter wheel soil mixing, penetration often uses water to homogenize and fluidize the soil, then a slurry with a relatively low water-to-cement ratio is injected on withdrawal. The dry method uses lighter equipment that can often work without platforms (timber mats may be needed on very soft ground). Dry binder is stored in a track-mounted delivery unit and delivered pneumatically to ports near the blades; the single-axis tool rotates rapidly, advances on penetration with air only to break up the soil, and binder is delivered during withdrawal mixing.
key_points: A wet-method slurry plant includes binder silos, slurry mixers, agitation tanks and pumps.
U.S. vertical-axis practice usually injects slurry on penetration so it is mixed on downstroke and upstroke.
Double-stroking and/or bottom dwell time help thorough mixing at the element base.
Cutter soil mixing: water on penetration, low water-to-cement-ratio slurry on withdrawal.
Dry method: air-only penetration, binder delivered pneumatically on withdrawal.
sections.applicability: Understanding deep mixing equipment and procedures for design and specification.

sections.title: Materials
sections.summary: The most common deep mixing binders in U.S. practice are cement and slag-cement blends for both wet and dry methods; lime and lime-cement columns have been installed by the dry method; potable water is typically used for wet-method slurry (p. 7-13).
sections.body: The most common binder materials in United States practice are cement and slag-cement blends for both the wet and dry methods of deep mixing. Lime and lime-cement columns have also been installed using the dry method. Potable water is typically used to make the slurry for the wet method (p. 7-13).
key_points: Cement and slag-cement blends are the most common binders for wet and dry methods.
Lime and lime-cement columns have been installed by the dry method.
Potable water is typically used for wet-method slurry.

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.summary: Key deep mixing design considerations: line, grade and loading; settlement and factor of safety targets; surface and subsurface conditions incl. water content, organic content, obstructions and bearing layer; prior experience; bench-scale trials; field trials and demonstration elements; layout; iterative analyses (pp. 7-14 to 7-15).
sections.body: Key design considerations after the feasibility assessment (pp. 7-14 to 7-15): line, grade and loading; desired performance in settlement control and factor of safety against instability; existing surface conditions (topography, drainage, land use, utilities and facilities); and subsurface conditions, including stratigraphy with attention to weak layers, water content (for thoroughly mixed soils, the binder needed for a target strength increases with water content, while low water content plastic clays are hard to mix but pretreatment with water instead of slurry helps), organic content and type (finely divided organic colloids interfere with cementitious reactions more than fibrous organics and peat; slag-cement blends tend to give stronger mixtures than pure cement at the same binder factor in organic soils), buried logs, stumps and obstructions, and the depth, variability and consistency of the bearing layer. Further considerations: prior deep mixing experience in similar soils; bench-scale trials during design to confirm treatability and inform bidders; whether a field trial is needed during design (usually not) and whether demonstration elements are needed at the start of construction (usually so); selecting a configuration, which for embankments usually means isolated elements under the central portion and shear walls perpendicular to the centerline under the side slopes; iterative analyses to optimize configuration and strength, accounting for multiple failure modes and variability of field-mixed soil-cement; and developing plans and specifications.
key_points: Binder needed for a target strength increases with soil water content.
Finely divided organics interfere with cementitious reactions more than fibrous organics.
Slag-cement blends tend to outperform pure cement at the same binder factor in organic soils.
Field trial during design: usually not needed; demonstration elements at start of construction: usually needed.
Embankments: isolated elements under the center, shear walls perpendicular to centerline under side slopes.
sections.applicability: Planning the data and decisions needed for a deep mixing design.

sections.title: Design Steps
sections.summary: Introduces the seven deep mixing design steps from the FHWA (2013) manual: project requirements, subsurface conditions, trial soil-cement properties, trial geometry, settlement, stability, and plans and specifications (pp. 7-15 to 7-18).
sections.body: As described in the FHWA (2013) deep mixing manual, design includes seven steps addressing the key design considerations (p. 7-15): (1) establish project requirements; (2) establish representative subsurface conditions; (3) establish trial soil-cement property values; (4) establish trial deep mixed geometry; (5) evaluate settlement; (6) evaluate stability; and (7) prepare the plans and specifications. Steps 3 through 6 are iterated until the performance criteria are met.
key_points: Seven steps, from FHWA (2013).
Steps 3 through 6 are iterated before plans and specifications are prepared.
sections.applicability: Deep mixing support of embankments, walls, abutments and other structures on soft ground in transportation projects.

sections.title: Step 1: Establish Project Requirements
sections.summary: Design Step 1 for deep mixing: establish the line, grade and loading of the proposed construction and the desired performance in terms of settlement and factor of safety, which become the criteria the Step 5 and 6 analyses are checked against (p. 7-15).
sections.body: This step includes establishing line, grade, loading, and desired performance in terms of settlement and factor of safety (p. 7-15). These performance criteria are what the settlement and stability results of Steps 5 and 6 are compared against.
key_points: Establish line, grade and loading.
Set settlement and factor of safety performance criteria.
sections.applicability: Deep mixing support of embankments, walls, abutments and other structures on soft ground in transportation projects.

sections.title: Step 2: Establish Representative Subsurface Conditions
sections.summary: Design Step 2 for deep mixing: determine stratigraphy, soil property values and the likelihood of obstructions, plus treatability indicators such as particle size distribution, Atterberg limits, water content, organic content and whether organics are finely divided or fibrous (p. 7-16).
sections.body: This step includes determining the stratigraphy, soil property values, and the likelihood of encountering obstructions during field mixing (p. 7-16). Besides engineering properties such as strength and compressibility of the untreated soil, other characteristics are important for estimating treatability: particle size distribution, Atterberg limits, water content, organic content, and whether the organics are finely divided or fibrous.
key_points: Determine stratigraphy, soil properties and likelihood of obstructions.
Treatability indicators: gradation, Atterberg limits, water content, organic content and organic type.
sections.applicability: Deep mixing support of embankments, walls, abutments and other structures on soft ground in transportation projects.

sections.title: Step 3: Establish Trial Soil-Cement Property Values
sections.summary: Design Step 3 for deep mixing: estimate design strength and modulus of field-mixed soil-cement; achievable strength falls with higher water and organic content; mixing is easiest in loose sands; modulus from tests or correlation with UCS; consider strength variability per FHWA (p. 7-16).
sections.body: This step estimates the design strength and modulus of field-mixed soil-cement (p. 7-16). Practically achievable strengths tend to decrease as the untreated soil water content increases, as the organic content increases, and when the organics are finely divided. Thorough mixing is easiest for loose sands and silty sands, more difficult for plastic clays, and can be challenging for stiff plastic clays; pretreating plastic clays by mixing with water before mixing with slurry can make thorough mixing easier. The soil-cement modulus can be measured in laboratory tests or estimated from correlations with unconfined compressive strength. Practically achievable strengths can be estimated from bench-scale treatability tests and experience on prior projects in similar materials. Strength variability should also be considered, with guidance in the FHWA manual.
key_points: Achievable strength decreases with higher water content, higher organic content and finely divided organics.
Mixing is easiest in loose sands and silty sands; harder in plastic clays; challenging in stiff plastic clays.
Modulus from laboratory tests or correlation with unconfined compressive strength.
Estimate achievable strength from bench-scale tests and prior project experience.
Consider strength variability (guidance in FHWA 2013).
sections.applicability: Deep mixing support of embankments, walls, abutments and other structures on soft ground in transportation projects.

sections.title: Step 4: Establish Trial Deep Mixed Geometry
sections.summary: Design Step 4 for deep mixing: set the layout pattern, area replacement ratio in each zone and treatment depth; an efficient embankment layout uses isolated elements under the center and overlapping elements forming shear walls under the side slopes, perpendicular to the alignment (p. 7-16).
sections.body: This step establishes the general layout pattern and the area replacement ratio in different zones beneath the embankment, as well as the treatment depth (p. 7-16). A generally efficient layout for embankment support uses isolated elements beneath the central portion of the embankment and overlapping elements forming continuous shear walls beneath the side slopes. The shear walls are oriented perpendicular to the embankment alignment to provide stability for the side slopes.
key_points: Define layout pattern, area replacement ratio by zone, and treatment depth.
Isolated elements under the embankment center; continuous shear walls under the side slopes.
Shear walls run perpendicular to the embankment alignment.
sections.applicability: Deep mixing support of embankments, walls, abutments and other structures on soft ground in transportation projects.

sections.title: Step 5: Evaluate Settlement
sections.summary: Design Step 5 for deep mixing: compute compression of the treated zone as a composite of soil-cement elements and untreated soil, add compression of underlying layers computed as for floating pile groups; a low embankment may need a load transfer platform (p. 7-16).
sections.body: Settlement is usually evaluated by calculating the compression of the zone treated by deep mixing and then adding the compression of the underlying soil layers (p. 7-16). The treated zone is treated as a composite of the soil-cement elements and the untreated soil. Compression of the underlying layers can be calculated in the same way as compression of soil under 'floating' pile groups. If the embankment is low-height, a load transfer platform may be necessary (see Chapter 6).
key_points: Settlement = compression of treated composite zone + compression of underlying layers.
Underlying layers are treated as under a floating pile group.
Low embankments may need a load transfer platform (Chapter 6).
sections.applicability: Deep mixing support of embankments, walls, abutments and other structures on soft ground in transportation projects.

sections.title: Step 6: Evaluate Stability
sections.summary: Design Step 6 for deep mixing: check seven failure modes (a)-(g), from sliding above, beneath or through the treated zone to shear wall overturning/bearing, toe crushing, vertical shear and extrusion; then compare Steps 5-6 results with Step 1 criteria and adjust depth, area ratio or strength (p. 7-17).
sections.body: All potential failure modes must be evaluated to ensure adequate factors of safety (p. 7-17): (a) sliding of the embankment above the deep mixed zone; (b) sliding beneath the deep mixed zone; (c) sliding on surfaces through the deep mixed zone; (d) combined overturning of the shear walls and bearing capacity of the soil beneath their toe; (e) crushing of the shear wall toe when founded on a hard stratum; (f) shearing on vertical planes in the shear walls beneath the side slopes; and (g) extrusion of soil between parallel shear walls beneath the side slopes. Modes (a) through (c) can be evaluated with a limit equilibrium slope stability program, using appropriate composite shear strengths in each treated zone for mode (c); the FHWA manual describes methods for (d) through (g). Results of Steps 5 and 6 are compared with the Step 1 criteria. If settlements are too large or factors of safety too low, the design is made more robust by deepening elements, increasing area replacement ratio(s) and/or increasing soil-cement strength, with attention to the practically achievable strength (Step 3). If criteria are met by wide margins, depths, ratios or strength can be decreased to optimize cost.
key_points: Seven failure modes (a)-(g) must be checked.
Modes (a)-(c) by limit equilibrium, with composite strengths in treated zones for (c).
Modes (d)-(g) by methods in the FHWA (2013) manual.
Remedies: deeper elements, higher area replacement ratio, higher strength (within achievable limits).
sections.applicability: Deep mixing support of embankments, walls, abutments and other structures on soft ground in transportation projects.

sections.title: Step 7: Prepare the Plans and Specifications
sections.summary: Design Step 7 for deep mixing: after iterating Steps 3-6, prepare plans and specifications that leave means and methods to the contractor, specify minimum area replacement ratios, and use a statistically based strength specification, e.g., 2% of elements cored, 4 of 5 specimens and 90% overall passing (pp. 7-17 to 7-18).
sections.body: Once the design is finalized by iterating on Steps 3 through 6, the plans and specifications are prepared (pp. 7-17 to 7-18). They should give the contractor wide latitude in means and methods while requiring the specified outcomes. For example, specifying minimum area replacement ratios rather than specific element sizes and spacings is preferred, although limits on maximum spacing and minimum diameters and widths are needed. Strength should be specified statistically: a typical transportation specification might require that 2% of elements be cored and tested, that 4 out of 5 specimens from each cored hole have an unconfined compressive strength at least equal to the specified strength, and that 90% of specimens for the entire project exhibit at least this strength. For this to be effective, the specifications must also require contractor quality control reports from calibrated data acquisition systems for every installed element so the owner or engineer can check for atypical installations. Geometric accuracy requirements are also included.
key_points: Specify outcomes, not means and methods.
Prefer minimum area replacement ratios, with limits on maximum spacing and minimum diameters and widths.
Typical: 2% of elements cored; 4 of 5 specimens per core at or above specified UCS; 90% of project specimens passing.
Require calibrated data acquisition records for every element.
sections.applicability: Writing deep mixing plans and end-result specifications.

sections.body: Primary references for design of deep mixing support systems for transportation applications (p. 7-18): FHWA (2013), Design Manual: Deep Mixing for Embankment and Foundation Support, Rep. No. FHWA-HRT-13-046 (Bruce et al.); Kitazume and Terashi (2013), The Deep Mixing Method; and the deep mixing section of the GeoTechTools website.
key_points: FHWA (2013) FHWA-HRT-13-046 is the main design reference.

sections.title: Overview of Construction Specifications and Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Container section on deep mixing specifications and QA: specification development (end-result specifications, the FHWA guide specification), a summary of quality assurance (submittals, observations, coring and strength acceptance), and instrumentation, monitoring and construction control (pp. 7-18 to 7-22).
sections.body: This section covers specification development (2.4.1), a summary of quality assurance (2.4.2), and a summary of instrumentation, monitoring and construction control (2.4.3) for deep mixing, pp. 7-18 to 7-22.
sections.applicability: Deep mixing support of embankments, walls, abutments and other structures on soft ground in transportation projects.

sections.title: Specification Development
sections.summary: A deep mixing guide specification is in FHWA (2013), with an updated version at GeoTechTools; all adapted specifications must be carefully edited. Deep mixing uses end-result specifications for geometry, mixing thoroughness and strength, with plan geometry specified in a normalized way (p. 7-18).
sections.body: A guide specification is available in the FHWA (2013) deep mixing report, and an updated version is available at GeoTechTools. Any guide specification or specification adapted from another project should be very carefully reviewed and edited for each new project (p. 7-18). Deep mixing specifications are end-result specifications in which the required geometry, thoroughness of mixing and strength of the improved ground are specified. Because contractors use different equipment and procedures, specifying means and methods is neither advisable nor possible. Even the plan view geometry is typically specified in a normalized fashion so that different size elements, within a specified range, can be used.
key_points: Guide specification in FHWA (2013); updated version at GeoTechTools.
End-result specifications: geometry, thoroughness of mixing, strength.
Plan geometry specified in normalized form so element sizes may vary within a range.
sections.applicability: Developing deep mixing specifications.

sections.title: Summary of Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Deep mixing QA: review contractor submittals (qualifications, bench-scale report, field demonstration elements cored top to bottom, work plan, QC plan, daily and summary reports), observe operations, select elements to core and representative specimens, and verify geometry, mixing and statistical strength criteria (pp. 7-19 to 7-20).
sections.body: Key elements of a thorough QA program (pp. 7-19 to 7-20): careful review of contractor submittals, including personnel qualifications (with an independent testing subcontractor); the contractor's own bench-scale mixing report, focused on mix designs suited to its equipment; a field demonstration element report, with test elements built before production and typically all cored top to bottom to determine thoroughness of mixing (defined as percent recovery of soil-cement per core run) and strength; a work plan; a QC plan; daily reports giving for each element its identification, location, top and bottom elevations, start and completion time, and logs versus depth of verticality, binder delivery rate, penetration/withdrawal rates, rotation rates and bottom treatment; and summary reports. The owner/engineer observes materials handling, slurry preparation and testing, mixing, coring, sampling, specimen storage and testing; selects the elements to be cored and the specimens to test, choosing specimens proportionately representative of the elements (a 3-inch specimen with a 1-inch clod of unmixed soil would not represent a 4-foot column unless the column held a boulder-sized clod); and checks geometry (plan dimensions, verticality, top and bottom elevations, overlap), thoroughness of mixing (specified minimum core recovery after excluding untreated material) and strength. Strength criteria are typically statistical, such as 80% of tests from each cored element and 90% of tests for the project exceeding the specified value; modern specifications typically do not require every result to meet a minimum.
key_points: The contractor performs its own bench-scale mixing program even if the owner has done one.
Demonstration elements are typically cored top to bottom.
Specimens must be proportionately representative of the element.
Typical strength acceptance: 80% per cored element and 90% project-wide exceeding the specified value.
sections.applicability: Planning QA for deep mixing construction.

sections.title: Summary of Instrumentation, Monitoring, and Construction Control
sections.summary: Deep mixing QC/QA relies on demonstrated means and methods repeated on production elements, plus coring of selected elements. Lists calibration, redundant sensors, binder reconciliation, slurry tests, records, drilling index, wet-grab samples, core recovery criteria (80-85% per run, 90% overall), 4-of-5 UCS testing, failure options and televiewers (pp. 7-20 to 7-22).
sections.body: The QC/QA philosophy is that the contractor demonstrates suitable materials, means and methods on heavily tested validation elements, observed by the owner/engineer, and then controls and documents that the same practices are used on production elements; the owner/engineer also selects a limited number of production elements for full-depth coring and testing, mostly tested by the contractor's laboratory and some by the owner/engineer (p. 7-20). Activities (pp. 7-21 to 7-22): calibration of all transducers and instruments; redundant systems for depth, rotation rate and penetration rate; reconciling delivery tickets with binder used; weighing dry binder and water for slurry; mud balance and Marsh funnel viscosity tests; geometric records; records of binder delivery, penetration/withdrawal and rotation rates, bottom treatment and sometimes power consumption, from which a drilling index (power consumption divided by penetration rate) can indicate penetration into a bearing layer; wet-grab samples for early strength indication, though acceptance is ordinarily by full-depth core recovery and UCS tests; core logs, with recovery of at least 80% or 85% of well mixed soil-cement per core run and 90% overall per boring; UCS tests on 5 representative specimens per core boring, 4 of 5 to meet the specified strength and 90% project-wide; standard options when an element fails, such as a second boring with 10 specimens of which 8 must pass, then a remediation plan for the shift's elements; optical televiewer logs with wet-grab samples where coarse particles prevent coring, with triple-tube wire-line coring giving some of the best core; and protection and trimming of the soil-cement.
key_points: Drilling index example: power consumption divided by penetration rate.
Core recovery: at least 80% or 85% well mixed soil-cement per core run; 90% overall per boring.
UCS: 5 specimens per core boring, 4 of 5 passing; 90% of production specimens passing project-wide.
Second core boring after a failure may need 10 specimens with 8 passing.
Triple-tube wire-line coring has given some of the best core results.
sections.applicability: Construction control and acceptance testing of deep mixed elements.

sections.title: Cost Data
sections.summary: Factors influencing deep mixing cost: wet vs dry method, treatment volume, element depths, specified UCS (recent projects about 100 psi to 500 psi, lower end most common), soil types, embedment into a hard layer, environmental conditions, binder availability, field trials, access, mobilization and QC/QA requirements (pp. 7-22 to 7-23).
sections.body: Factors that influence the cost of deep mixing projects (pp. 7-22 to 7-23): wet versus dry method; treatment volume; typical and maximum element depths; the specified unconfined compressive strength, which on recent projects has varied from about 100 psi to 500 psi, with the lower end of this range most common; soil types to be treated; depth of embedment into a hard bearing layer; environmental conditions requiring special health and safety precautions and/or off-site disposal of spoils; availability of binder materials; extent of field trial testing; site access; mobilization/demobilization cost; and normal versus excessively restrictive QC/QA requirements.
key_points: Specified UCS on recent projects: about 100 psi to 500 psi, lower end most common (p. 7-23).
Excessively restrictive QC/QA requirements raise cost.
sections.applicability: Estimating and controlling deep mixing cost.

sections.title: Cost Components
sections.summary: Typical deep mixing cost components from FHWA (2013): wet-method mobilization $80,000 to $150,000 per rig (site 200 miles from the contractor's yard), unit cost $75 to $115 per cubic yard, QC/QA participation 3% to 5%, engineering about 10%; recent mobilization can exceed $150,000; dry method cheaper (p. 7-23).
sections.body: According to the FHWA (2013) deep mixing manual (p. 7-23), mobilization/demobilization for the wet method can be $80,000 to $150,000 per mixing rig, including support equipment, for a site 200 miles from a qualified contractor's yard; unit costs can range from $75 to $115 per cubic yard, with lower costs sometimes on large projects in competitive markets; the contractor's QC/QA participation can be estimated at 3% to 5% of production deep mixing costs; and engineering for design and construction services may be about 10% of deep mixing construction cost. Actual costs depend heavily on market conditions, project size, ground conditions and project-specific constraints. Recent information indicates mobilization/demobilization can exceed $150,000 per rig and associated support equipment. Mobilization and unit costs for the dry method are typically less than for the wet method, though the dry method applies to a narrower range of conditions and project types.
key_points: Wet-method mobilization/demobilization: $80,000 to $150,000 per rig (recently can exceed $150,000).
Unit cost: $75 to $115 per cubic yard.
QC/QA participation: 3% to 5% of production cost; engineering: about 10%.
Dry method costs are typically lower but it applies more narrowly.
sections.applicability: Preliminary cost estimates for deep mixing.

sections.title: Mass Mixing
sections.summary: Part 3 on mass mixing: read deep mixing first; mass mixing has 100% or nearly 100% coverage, lower design strength and shallower treatment, and includes shallow soil mixing (large vertical-axis shafts) and mass stabilization (excavator-mounted horizontal drum) (pp. 7-24 to 7-40).
sections.body: Because mass mixing and deep mixing are so closely related with no distinct boundary, a person interested in mass mixing should first learn about deep mixing, then read this part and consult the mass mixing section of GeoTechTools (p. 7-24). Mass mixing differs from deep mixing in that (1) area coverage is 100% or nearly 100%, whereas deep mixing coverage is typically much less than 100%; (2) design strength is typically lower; and (3) treatment depth is typically less. Mass mixing includes shallow soil mixing, done with large-diameter vertical-axis rotating shafts with mixing blades, and mass stabilization, done with a horizontal-axis mixing drum mounted on the stick of an excavator. Part 3.0 covers feasibility, construction and materials, design with a worked example, specifications and QA, cost data and a case history.
key_points: Learn deep mixing first; then read for differences.
Mass mixing: 100% or nearly 100% coverage, lower design strength, shallower treatment.
Two forms: shallow soil mixing and mass stabilization.
sections.applicability: Mass mixing (shallow soil mixing and mass stabilization) of soft ground at 100% or nearly 100% coverage in transportation projects.

sections.title: Feasibility Considerations
sections.summary: Mass mixing suits applications benefiting from wide coverage at 100% or nearly 100% replacement ratio where lower strengths than deep mixing are acceptable; its uniformity is operator dependent and strength variability may exceed that of well-controlled deep mixing (p. 7-24).
sections.body: Mass mixing is usually intended for applications that benefit from wide coverage at a 100% or nearly 100% replacement ratio, but for which strengths lower than typically specified for deep mixing are acceptable (p. 7-24). The uniformity of mass mixed soil-cement is operator dependent, and strength variability may be greater than for well-controlled deep mixing operations. Subsections cover applications, advantages and disadvantages, feasibility evaluations, limitations and alternatives.
key_points: Wide coverage at 100% or nearly 100% replacement ratio with lower strengths.
Uniformity is operator dependent; strength variability may be greater than deep mixing.
sections.applicability: Mass mixing (shallow soil mixing and mass stabilization) of soft ground at 100% or nearly 100% coverage in transportation projects.

sections.title: Applications
sections.summary: Mass mixing limits settlement and increases shear strength of roadway and railway embankment foundations, supports storage tanks, stabilizes excavations, serves land reclamation and contaminant fixation, and forms load transfer and working platforms over deep mixed elements (Figure 7-5) (p. 7-24).
sections.body: Mass mixing has proven effective at limiting settlement and increasing the shear strength of roadway and railway embankment foundation soils. It has also been used to support structures such as petroleum storage tanks, to stabilize excavations, in land reclamation projects, and for contaminant fixation (p. 7-24). Mass mixing has been used to create load transfer platforms over deep mixed elements that carry the transferred loads to more competent materials at depth (Figure 7-5, p. 7-25). The mass mixed load transfer platform also serves as a construction working platform for installing the deep mixed elements and for later construction.
key_points: Limits settlement and increases shear strength under roadway and railway embankments.
Used for tanks, excavation stabilization, land reclamation and contaminant fixation.
Mass mixed platform over deep mixed elements acts as load transfer and working platform.
figures: Figure 7-5: Mass mixing to create a load-transfer platform and construction working platform.
sections.applicability: Mass mixing (shallow soil mixing and mass stabilization) of soft ground at 100% or nearly 100% coverage in transportation projects.

sections.title: Advantages and Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: Container section listing the principal advantages (3.1.2.1) and potential disadvantages (3.1.2.2) of mass mixing compared with deep mixing (pp. 7-25 to 7-26).
sections.body: This section compares mass mixing with deep mixing, listing advantages (Section 3.1.2.1) and potential disadvantages (Section 3.1.2.2), pp. 7-25 to 7-26.
sections.applicability: Mass mixing (shallow soil mixing and mass stabilization) of soft ground at 100% or nearly 100% coverage in transportation projects.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.summary: Principal advantages of mass mixing over deep mixing: typically less expensive per unit volume (though treatment volume per foot of depth is larger because of the larger area replacement ratio), and it can be done rapidly (p. 7-25).
sections.body: The principal advantages of mass mixing in comparison to deep mixing (p. 7-25) are that it is typically less expensive than deep mixing on a unit volume basis, although the treatment volume per foot of depth is larger because of the larger area replacement ratio, and that it can be done rapidly.
key_points: Less expensive per unit volume than deep mixing.
Larger treatment volume per foot of depth.
Can be done rapidly.
sections.applicability: Mass mixing (shallow soil mixing and mass stabilization) of soft ground at 100% or nearly 100% coverage in transportation projects.

sections.title: Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: Principal disadvantages of mass mixing: equipment cannot easily penetrate dense or stiff soils; mass stabilization depth limited to about 20 feet (shallow soil mixing 50 feet or more); QC records only total binder and mixing time per cell, so quality is more operator dependent (pp. 7-25 to 7-26).
sections.body: The principal disadvantages of mass mixing in comparison to deep mixing (pp. 7-25 to 7-26): mass mixing equipment cannot easily penetrate dense or stiff soils; the maximum treatment depth for mass stabilization (mixing drum on a backhoe stick) is limited to about 20 feet, whereas 'shallow' soil stabilization with large-diameter single-axis equipment can extend to 50 feet or more; and quality control, monitoring and documentation for mass stabilization are not usually as comprehensive as for modern deep mixing, because binder delivery and mixing energy at every plan location and depth in a cell are not typically monitored or recorded. Instead, only the total binder delivered and total mixing time in a treated cell are recorded, and the quality and uniformity of the product are more operator dependent than for deep mixing.
key_points: Cannot easily penetrate dense or stiff soils.
Mass stabilization limited to about 20 feet; shallow soil mixing can reach 50 feet or more.
Only total binder and total mixing time per cell are recorded for mass stabilization.
sections.applicability: Mass mixing (shallow soil mixing and mass stabilization) of soft ground at 100% or nearly 100% coverage in transportation projects.

sections.title: Feasibility Evaluations
sections.summary: Container section for mass mixing feasibility evaluations: geotechnical (soft organic soils, peat, soft clays and silts, hydraulic fill, sludges), environmental considerations (as for deep mixing), and site conditions (equipment space) (p. 7-26).
sections.body: Feasibility of mass mixing is evaluated under geotechnical conditions (Section 3.1.3.1), environmental considerations (Section 3.1.3.2) and site conditions (Section 3.1.3.3), on p. 7-26.
sections.applicability: Mass mixing (shallow soil mixing and mass stabilization) of soft ground at 100% or nearly 100% coverage in transportation projects.

sections.title: Geotechnical
sections.summary: Mass mixing applies to soft organic soils and peat, soft clays, soft silt, hydraulic fill and sludges; its equipment is generally not designed to penetrate stiff clays or dense sands, and logs, stumps or building debris prevent it from advancing (p. 7-26).
sections.body: Mass mixing is applicable in soft organic soils and peat, soft clays, soft silt, hydraulic fill, and sludges (p. 7-26). Mass mixing equipment is generally not designed to penetrate stiff clays or dense sands, whereas powerful wet-method deep mixing equipment can penetrate such materials. Obstructions such as logs, stumps or building debris will prevent mass mixing equipment from advancing.
key_points: Applicable soils: soft organic soils, peat, soft clays, soft silt, hydraulic fill, sludges.
Not designed to penetrate stiff clays or dense sands.
Logs, stumps and building debris stop mass mixing equipment.
sections.applicability: Mass mixing (shallow soil mixing and mass stabilization) of soft ground at 100% or nearly 100% coverage in transportation projects.

sections.title: Environmental Considerations
sections.summary: Environmental considerations for mass mixing are essentially those for deep mixing, but with 100% area coverage mass mixing can stabilize contaminants over the entire treatment area (p. 7-26).
sections.body: The environmental considerations for mass mixing are essentially the same as for deep mixing (cement immobilization of contaminants, freezing conditions, freeze-thaw above the frost depth), although with 100% area coverage, mass mixing can stabilize contaminants over the entire treatment area (p. 7-26).
key_points: Same environmental considerations as deep mixing.
100% coverage stabilizes contaminants over the whole treated area.
sections.applicability: Mass mixing (shallow soil mixing and mass stabilization) of soft ground at 100% or nearly 100% coverage in transportation projects.

sections.title: Site Conditions
sections.summary: Site-condition feasibility for mass mixing is similar to deep mixing; wet-method shallow soil mixing with large single-axis shafts needs more equipment space than dry-method mass stabilization with a horizontal-axis drum (p. 7-26).
sections.body: Feasibility considerations regarding site conditions for mass mixing are similar to those for deep mixing (p. 7-26). Shallow soil mixing operations, using large-diameter single-axis rotating shafts with mixing blades and the wet method, require more equipment space than mass stabilization operations using a horizontal-axis mixing drum and the dry method.
key_points: Similar site considerations to deep mixing.
Wet shallow soil mixing needs more space than dry mass stabilization.
sections.applicability: Mass mixing (shallow soil mixing and mass stabilization) of soft ground at 100% or nearly 100% coverage in transportation projects.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.summary: Limitations of mass mixing: treatment depths typically about 50 feet for shallow soil mixing equipment and about 20 feet for mass stabilization equipment; it cannot penetrate dense or stiff soils, cobbles, boulders or obstructions; buried utilities limit use (p. 7-26).
sections.body: Limitations of mass mixing (p. 7-26): treatment depths are typically limited to about 50 feet for shallow soil mixing equipment and to about 20 feet for mass stabilization equipment; and mass mixing equipment typically cannot penetrate dense or stiff soils, cobbles, boulders or other obstructions, while buried utilities or structures can limit its application.
key_points: Depth: about 50 feet (shallow soil mixing), about 20 feet (mass stabilization).
Cannot penetrate dense or stiff soils, cobbles, boulders or obstructions.
sections.applicability: Mass mixing (shallow soil mixing and mass stabilization) of soft ground at 100% or nearly 100% coverage in transportation projects.

sections.title: Alternative Solutions (or Technologies)
sections.summary: Alternatives to mass mixing: excavation and replacement where poor soils are of limited depth and groundwater is absent or controllable; for deeper poor soils compared with shallow soil mixing, the alternatives listed for deep mixing (pp. 7-26 to 7-27).
sections.body: When poor quality soils extend only to a limited depth, excavation and replacement can be an expedient alternative to mass mixing, provided groundwater does not interfere with excavation or can be controlled (p. 7-26). When poor soils extend deeper, and the comparison is to the 'shallow' soil mixing method, the alternative technologies listed for deep mixing (prefabricated vertical drains with preloading, densification, and column-supported embankments) can be considered (p. 7-27).
key_points: Excavation and replacement for shallow poor soils if groundwater is controllable.
For deeper soils, consider the deep mixing alternatives.
sections.applicability: Mass mixing (shallow soil mixing and mass stabilization) of soft ground at 100% or nearly 100% coverage in transportation projects.

sections.body: This section describes construction by shallow soil mixing and mass stabilization (Section 3.2.1) and the materials used (Section 3.2.2), p. 7-27.

sections.title: Construction
sections.summary: Container heading for mass mixing construction methods: shallow soil mixing (3.2.1.1) with large-diameter single-shaft equipment, and mass stabilization (3.2.1.2) with a horizontal-axis drum on an excavator stick (p. 7-27).
sections.body: Mass mixing is constructed either by shallow soil mixing (Section 3.2.1.1) or by mass stabilization (Section 3.2.1.2), described on p. 7-27.
