sections.title: Shallow Soil Mixing
sections.summary: Shallow soil mixing uses large-diameter (about 10 feet) single-shaft equipment to make overlapping columns for complete or nearly complete coverage, usually with pumped slurry (dry binder in very soft ground), and needs working platforms; it is not surface stabilization (p. 7-27).
sections.body: Shallow soil mixing generally uses relatively large-diameter (about 10 feet), single-shaft mixing equipment, arranged to create a series of overlapping columns giving complete or nearly complete coverage (p. 7-27). It most often uses pumped slurry, requiring a slurry plant similar to that for wet-method deep mixing; in very soft ground or sludges dry binder can be delivered pneumatically. Either way, the binder is conveyed through the mixing shaft to the mixing blades. Working platforms and/or timber mats are necessary for the equipment on soft surfaces. Shallow soil mixing is not surface stabilization, in which soil and binder are blended typically to a depth of 1 foot or less and compacted in lifts.
key_points: Shaft diameter about 10 feet; overlapping columns.
Usually pumped slurry; dry binder in very soft ground or sludges.
Not surface stabilization (1 foot or less, compacted in lifts).
sections.applicability: Mass mixing (shallow soil mixing and mass stabilization) of soft ground at 100% or nearly 100% coverage in transportation projects.

sections.title: Mass Stabilization
sections.summary: Mass stabilization uses a horizontal-axis mixing drum on an excavator stick, with slurry or dry binder; contiguous rectangular cells are marked and each fully treated before the next, the operator moving the drum vertically and horizontally in multiple passes (p. 7-27).
sections.body: Mass stabilization employs a horizontal-axis mixing drum attached to the stick of an excavator, with binder in slurry or dry form delivered to the drum (p. 7-27). Contiguous rectangular cells are marked with cord or by other means, and each cell is fully treated before moving to the next. The operator moves the rotating drum vertically and horizontally to achieve treatment, typically making multiple passes through each point in the cell.
key_points: Excavator-mounted horizontal-axis drum.
Contiguous rectangular cells treated one at a time.
Multiple passes through each point in a cell.
sections.applicability: Mass mixing (shallow soil mixing and mass stabilization) of soft ground at 100% or nearly 100% coverage in transportation projects.

sections.title: Materials
sections.summary: The materials used for mass mixing are typically the same as for deep mixing: cement and slag-cement blends most commonly in U.S. practice, lime or lime-cement by the dry method, and potable water for slurry (p. 7-27).
sections.body: The materials used for mass mixing are typically the same as for deep mixing (p. 7-27), that is, the binders and water described in Section 2.2.2: cement and slag-cement blends most commonly, lime or lime-cement with the dry method, and potable water for slurry.
key_points: Same materials as deep mixing.
sections.applicability: Mass mixing (shallow soil mixing and mass stabilization) of soft ground at 100% or nearly 100% coverage in transportation projects.

sections.title: Design
sections.summary: Mass mixing design is similar to deep mixing design except that several deep mixing failure modes need not be considered, and mass mixed soil-cement strength may be more variable than deep mixed soil-cement built with good QC (p. 7-27).
sections.body: The design process for mass mixing is similar to that for deep mixing, except that several failure modes for deep mixed systems do not need to be considered. The strength of mass mixed soil-cement may also be more variable than that of deep mixed soil-cement constructed with good quality control (p. 7-27). The section covers design considerations, the design procedure, a design example and primary design references.
key_points: Fewer failure modes than deep mixing.
Strength may be more variable than well-controlled deep mixing.
sections.applicability: Mass mixing (shallow soil mixing and mass stabilization) of soft ground at 100% or nearly 100% coverage in transportation projects.

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.summary: Mass mixing design considerations are similar to deep mixing, except that coverage is complete or nearly complete, so no decisions about isolated elements, shear walls or grid arrangements are needed (p. 7-28).
sections.body: Design considerations for mass mixing are similar to those for deep mixing (Section 2.3.1), except that the coverage area is complete or nearly complete, so it is not necessary to decide on the use of isolated elements, shear walls or grid arrangements (p. 7-28).
key_points: No need to choose isolated elements, shear walls or grids.
sections.applicability: Mass mixing (shallow soil mixing and mass stabilization) of soft ground at 100% or nearly 100% coverage in transportation projects.

sections.title: Design Procedure
sections.summary: Introduces the seven-step mass mixing design procedure, similar to deep mixing; with 100% or nearly 100% coverage there is no need to check safety against vertical shearing or extrusion (p. 7-28).
sections.body: The design procedure for mass mixing is similar to that for deep mixing, with the steps listed in the following subsections (p. 7-28). Because 100% or nearly 100% area coverage is provided, it is not necessary to check for safety against vertical shearing or extrusion.
key_points: Same seven steps as deep mixing.
No vertical shearing or extrusion checks needed at 100% or nearly 100% coverage.
sections.applicability: Mass mixing (shallow soil mixing and mass stabilization) of soft ground at 100% or nearly 100% coverage in transportation projects.

sections.title: Step 1: Establish Project Requirements
sections.summary: Mass mixing design Step 1 is the same as for deep mixing: establish the line, grade and loading and the desired performance in terms of settlement and factor of safety (p. 7-28).
sections.body: This step is the same as for deep mixing (p. 7-28): establish line, grade, loading, and desired performance in terms of settlement and factor of safety (Section 2.3.2.1).
key_points: Same as deep mixing Step 1.
sections.applicability: Mass mixing (shallow soil mixing and mass stabilization) of soft ground at 100% or nearly 100% coverage in transportation projects.

sections.title: Step 2: Establish Representative Subsurface Conditions
sections.summary: Mass mixing design Step 2 is the same as for deep mixing: determine stratigraphy, soil property values, likelihood of obstructions, and treatability indicators such as water and organic content (p. 7-28).
sections.body: This step is the same as for deep mixing (p. 7-28): determine the stratigraphy, soil property values, likelihood of obstructions, and the characteristics that govern treatability (Section 2.3.2.2).
key_points: Same as deep mixing Step 2.
sections.applicability: Mass mixing (shallow soil mixing and mass stabilization) of soft ground at 100% or nearly 100% coverage in transportation projects.

sections.title: Step 3: Establish Trial Soil-Cement Property Values
sections.summary: Mass mixing design Step 3 involves the same considerations as deep mixing, but because area coverage is 100% or nearly 100%, lower strengths are generally used, and mass mixed strength is generally more variable than modern deep mixing (p. 7-28).
sections.body: This step involves the same considerations as for deep mixing (p. 7-28). However, because the percent area coverage is large (100% or nearly 100%), lower strengths are generally used for mass mixing than for deep mixing. It should also be recognized at this stage that the strength of soil-cement produced by mass mixing is generally more variable than that produced by modern deep mixing methods.
key_points: Lower design strengths than deep mixing.
Strength generally more variable than modern deep mixing.
sections.applicability: Mass mixing (shallow soil mixing and mass stabilization) of soft ground at 100% or nearly 100% coverage in transportation projects.

sections.title: Step 4: Establish Trial Mass Mixed Geometry
sections.summary: Mass mixing Step 4: 100% coverage with single columns needs spacing-to-diameter ratios of 0.707 (square) or 0.866 (triangular), with overlap areas of 57% and 21%; 98% coverage in a triangular array needs 0.929 with 7% overlap; treatment depth also set (p. 7-28).
sections.body: For vertical-axis single-column elements, 100% coverage can be achieved with spacing-to-diameter ratios of 0.707 for a square array and 0.866 for an equilateral triangular array (p. 7-28). The corresponding column overlap areas are 57% and 21% of the treated areas for square and triangular arrays, so equilateral triangular arrays are more efficient than square arrays. In many situations 100% coverage may not be necessary; for example, if 98% coverage is acceptable for a triangular array, the necessary spacing-to-diameter ratio is 0.929, and the column overlap areas are only 7% of the treated area. The mass mixing geometry also includes the treatment depth, which may be important for stability and settlement control.
key_points: 100% coverage: s/d = 0.707 (square array), 0.866 (equilateral triangular array).
Overlap areas: 57% (square) and 21% (triangular) of treated area.
98% coverage, triangular: s/d = 0.929 with 7% overlap.
Triangular arrays are more efficient than square arrays.
sections.applicability: Mass mixing (shallow soil mixing and mass stabilization) of soft ground at 100% or nearly 100% coverage in transportation projects.

sections.title: Step 5: Evaluate Settlement
sections.summary: Mass mixing Step 5: settlement is evaluated the same way as for deep mixing (compression of the treated zone plus underlying layers), but a separate load transfer platform would not be necessary in a mass mixing application (p. 7-29).
sections.body: Settlement is evaluated in the same way as for deep mixing (compression of the treated zone plus compression of underlying layers, Section 2.3.2.5). However, a separate load transfer platform would not be necessary in a mass mixing application (p. 7-29).
key_points: Same settlement approach as deep mixing.
No separate load transfer platform needed.
sections.applicability: Mass mixing (shallow soil mixing and mass stabilization) of soft ground at 100% or nearly 100% coverage in transportation projects.

sections.title: Step 6: Evaluate Stability
sections.summary: Mass mixing Step 6: failure modes (a) sliding above, (b) beneath and (c) through the mass mixed zone, and under lateral loading (d) overturning with toe bearing and (e) toe crushing on a hard stratum; (a)-(c) by limit equilibrium; then compare with Step 1 and adjust size, depth or strength (p. 7-29).
sections.body: This step is similar to the deep mixing stability evaluation but with fewer failure modes (p. 7-29). The principal modes are: (a) sliding of the embankment above the mass mixed zone; (b) sliding beneath it; (c) sliding on surfaces through it; (d) combined overturning of the mass mixed zone and bearing capacity of the soil beneath its toe if the zone is laterally loaded; and (e) crushing of the toe if the zone is founded on a hard stratum and laterally loaded. Modes (a) through (c) can be evaluated with a limit equilibrium slope stability program; the FHWA deep mixing manual describes methods easily adapted for (d) and (e). Results of Steps 5 and 6 are compared with the Step 1 criteria. If settlements are too large or factors of safety too low, the mass mixed zone is made larger or deeper and/or the soil-cement strength increased, considering the practically achievable strength (Step 3). If criteria are met by wide margins, treatment volume and/or strength can be reduced to optimize cost.
key_points: Five failure modes (a)-(e); (d) and (e) only under lateral loading.
Modes (a)-(c) by limit equilibrium slope stability analysis.
Remedies: larger or deeper zone, or higher strength within achievable limits.
sections.applicability: Mass mixing (shallow soil mixing and mass stabilization) of soft ground at 100% or nearly 100% coverage in transportation projects.

sections.title: Step 7: Prepare the Plans and Specifications
sections.summary: Mass mixing Step 7: after iterating Steps 3 through 6, prepare plans and specifications that give the contractor wide latitude in means and methods while requiring specified outcomes, with a statistically based strength specification (p. 7-29).
sections.body: Upon finalizing the design by iterating on Steps 3 through 6, the plans and specifications for construction can be prepared (p. 7-29). They should allow the contractor wide latitude in means and methods while still requiring that the specified outcomes be achieved. Regarding strength, a statistically based specification should be used.
key_points: Outcome-based specification.
Statistically based strength specification.
sections.applicability: Mass mixing (shallow soil mixing and mass stabilization) of soft ground at 100% or nearly 100% coverage in transportation projects.

sections.title: Design Example
sections.summary: Worked mass mixing design example (pp. 7-29 to 7-35): a 20-foot embankment with 2H:1V slopes on 15 feet of very soft silty organic soil, mass mixed to the bearing layer with dry slag-cement; covers properties, geometry, settlement and Spencer stability analyses.
sections.body: A design example (pp. 7-29 to 7-35) applies the seven-step procedure to an embankment on very soft silty organic soil treated by dry-method mass mixing. Steps 1 and 2 set the geometry, loads, soil properties and criteria; Step 3 derives soil-cement modulus and design shear strength; Step 4 fixes the mass mixed geometry; Step 5 estimates compression; Step 6 checks stability with infinite slope and Spencer's method analyses; Step 7 prepares plans and specifications.
key_points: Example of dry-method mass mixing under a 20-foot embankment.
Uses FHWA (2013) factors to convert specified field UCS to design shear strength.
sections.applicability: Mass mixing (shallow soil mixing and mass stabilization) of soft ground at 100% or nearly 100% coverage in transportation projects.

sections.title: Steps 1 and 2
sections.summary: Example Steps 1-2: 20-ft embankment, 2H:1V slopes, 70-ft crest, 250 psf traffic surcharge, on 15 ft of very soft silty organic soil (80 pcf, 50 psf) over a hard layer; fill 125 (unit weight), phi 33 deg; criteria FS 1.3 above, FS 1.5 through, settlement at most 2 in. (pp. 7-29 to 7-31).
sections.body: A 20-foot high embankment is proposed with 2H:1V side slopes and a 70-foot crest width, with a 250 psf traffic surcharge for design (p. 7-29). The subsurface consists of 15 feet of very soft silty organic soil over a hard bearing layer (Figure 7-6, p. 7-31). The embankment soil is compacted sandy silt with a unit weight of 125 (printed as 'psf' on p. 7-30; Figure 7-6 gives 125 lbs/ft3) and a friction angle of 33 degrees; the silty organic soil has a unit weight of 80 pcf and a shear strength of 50 psf. Design requirements: (1) factor of safety at least 1.3 for sliding entirely in the embankment above the soil-cement; (2) at least 1.5 for sliding through the embankment, the soil-cement and the silty organic soil beyond it; and (3) embankment settlement not more than 2 inches. The required values differ because the 33-degree friction angle is conservative and more reliable than the soil-cement strength estimate, and shallow sliding at the slope surface has smaller consequences than a large mass through the embankment, soil-cement and untreated soil (p. 7-30). Figure 7-6 tabulates mass mixing at 85 lbs/ft3 and undrained cohesion 930 psf.
key_points: Embankment 20 ft high, 2H:1V slopes, 70-ft crest; traffic surcharge 250 psf.
15 ft of very soft silty organic soil: 80 pcf, shear strength 50 psf, over hard bearing layer.
Fill: compacted sandy silt, 125 lbs/ft3 (Figure 7-6), friction angle 33 degrees.
Criteria: FS >= 1.3 above soil-cement; FS >= 1.5 through it; settlement <= 2 inches.
figures: Figure 7-6: Cross-section and material properties for design example.
sections.applicability: Worked example of setting project requirements and subsurface conditions for mass mixing.

sections.title: Step 3: Establish Trial Soil-Cement Property Values
sections.summary: Example Step 3: field UCS 26 psi (3700 psf) by dry method with slag-cement at binder factor 8.5 pcf; unit weight 80 to about 85 pcf; E50 = 150 qu, Poisson's ratio 0.1, M about 560,000 psf; design shear strength = (0.5)(0.8)(1.0)(0.63)(3700 psf) = 930 psf (p. 7-32).
sections.body: From published literature, a design-phase laboratory program and industry experts, a field-mixed unconfined compressive strength of 26 psi (3700 psf) was judged reliably and economically achievable by the dry method with a slag-cement blend at a binder factor of 8.5 pounds per cubic foot (p. 7-32). The specifications will require a UCS, not a binder factor, but the binder factor estimates the slight unit weight increase from about 80 pcf untreated to about 85 pcf. For settlement, the secant Young's modulus at 50% of UCS, E50, can be taken as 150 times the UCS per FHWA (2013), with Poisson's ratio 0.1. As printed: E50 = 150(26 psi) = 3,840 psi = 550,000 psf, and M = E50(1 - nu)/((1 + nu)(1 - 2nu)) = 560,000 psf, nearly the same as E50. For stability, FHWA (2013) applies four factors to the specified field strength: 0.5 to convert UCS to shear strength; 0.8 to convert peak unconfined strength to confined large-strain strength against progressive failure; a curing factor of 1.0 for 28 days; and a variability factor (FHWA 2013 Sections 5.4.8 and 6.1.3). Using a factor of 1.5, a coefficient of variation of 0.6 and a 70% probability that the actual strength equals or exceeds the desired field strength, the variability factor is 0.63 (FHWA 2013 Table 12). Design shear strength ssc = (0.5)(0.8)(1.0)(0.63)(3700 psf) = 930 psf. With 100% area coverage there is no reduction for area replacement ratio.
key_points: Field UCS 26 psi (3700 psf); dry method, slag-cement blend, binder factor 8.5 pcf.
Unit weight rises from about 80 pcf to about 85 pcf.
E50 = 150 x UCS; Poisson's ratio 0.1; printed E50 = 3,840 psi = 550,000 psf; M = 560,000 psf.
Design shear strength factors: 0.5 x 0.8 x 1.0 (28-day curing) x 0.63 (variability) = 930 psf.
Variability factor 0.63 for CV 0.6, 70% probability, factor 1.5 (FHWA 2013 Table 12).
No area replacement reduction at 100% coverage.
equations: Unnumbered equation, p. 7-32: E50 = 150(26 psi) = 3,840 psi = 550,000 psf; secant Young's modulus at 50% of UCS taken as 150 times the UCS (FHWA 2013). Values as printed.
Unnumbered equation, p. 7-32: M = E50 (1 - nu)/((1 + nu)(1 - 2 nu)) = (550,000 psf)(1 - 0.1)/((1 + 0.1)(1 - 2(0.1))) = 560,000 psf; constrained modulus from E50 and Poisson's ratio.

Unnumbered equation, p. 7-32: ssc = (0.5)(0.8)(1.0)(0.63)(3700 psf) = 930 psf; design shear strength of soil-cement from specified field UCS times conversion, large-strain, curing and variability factors.
sections.applicability: Converting a specified field UCS to design modulus and shear strength for mass mixed or deep mixed soil-cement.

sections.title: Step 4: Establish Trial Mass Mixed Geometry
sections.summary: Example Step 4: the trial mass mixed zone (Figure 7-6) extends from the ground surface down 15 feet to the hard bearing layer and 10 feet beyond the toe of the embankment (p. 7-33).
sections.body: The trial mass mixed geometry is shown in Figure 7-6. The mass mixing extends from the ground surface down 15 feet to the hard bearing layer, and it extends 10 feet beyond the toe of the embankment (p. 7-33). With 100% coverage the whole zone is treated as soil-cement.
key_points: Treated depth 15 ft to the bearing layer.
Treatment extends 10 ft beyond the embankment toe.
sections.applicability: Worked example of setting mass mixed treatment geometry.

sections.title: Step 5: Evaluate Settlement
sections.summary: Example Step 5: compression of the soil-cement = applied stress divided by modulus; constrained modulus near the center, small difference from E at nu = 0.1; (15 ft)((20 ft)(125 pcf) + 250 psf)/(550,000 psf) = 0.075 ft = 0.9 inch, under the 2-inch limit (p. 7-33).
sections.body: Compression of the soil-cement is calculated by dividing the applied stress by the appropriate modulus (p. 7-33). Near the embankment center compression is approximately one-dimensional and the constrained modulus applies; near the edge some shear distortion occurs, but the applied load is smaller. Because Poisson's ratio is small, the Young's and constrained moduli differ little. Using either value, compression of the soil-cement is less than 1.0 inch, e.g., (15 ft)((20 ft)(125 pcf) + 250 psf)/(550,000 psf) = 0.075 ft = 0.9 inches. If compression of the underlying bearing layer is also small, settlement will be less than the acceptable 2 inches.
key_points: Compression = thickness x applied stress / modulus.
Calculated compression 0.075 ft = 0.9 inch, below the 2-inch criterion.
equations: Unnumbered equation, p. 7-33: (15 ft)((20 ft)(125 pcf) + 250 psf)/(550,000 psf) = 0.075 ft = 0.9 inches; one-dimensional compression of the 15-ft soil-cement zone under embankment plus traffic surcharge.
sections.applicability: Worked example of a soil-cement compression estimate.

sections.title: Step 6: Evaluate Stability
sections.summary: Example Step 6: sliding above the soil-cement checked by infinite slope, FS = tan(33 deg)/0.5 = 1.3; sliding through embankment, soil-cement and untreated soil by Spencer's method gives FS 1.55 (circular) and 1.50 (non-circular), both acceptable (pp. 7-33 to 7-35).
sections.body: For the Figure 7-6 configuration, the only stability failure modes of concern are (1) sliding of the embankment above the soil-cement and (2) sliding through the embankment, the soil-cement and the silty organic soil beyond the treated zone (p. 7-33). For sliding above the soil-cement, the lowest factor of safety is the infinite slope value, tan(33 deg)/0.5 = 1.3, which is acceptable. Surfaces through the embankment, soil-cement and untreated soil were analyzed with Spencer's method, with thorough searches for critical circular and non-circular surfaces. The critical circular surface has a factor of safety of 1.55 (Figure 7-7, p. 7-34) and the critical non-circular surface 1.50 (Figure 7-8, p. 7-35), both acceptable under the Step 1 criteria. Because settlement and stability criteria are satisfied, no further iterations are necessary.
key_points: Infinite slope FS above soil-cement = tan(33 deg)/0.5 = 1.3.
Spencer's method: critical circular FS 1.55; critical non-circular FS 1.50.
Criteria satisfied; no further iteration.
equations: Unnumbered equation, p. 7-33: FS = tan(33 deg)/0.5 = 1.3; infinite slope factor of safety for the 2H:1V cohesionless embankment slope.
figures: Figure 7-7: Slope stability analysis results for circular sliding surfaces.
Figure 7-8: Slope stability analysis results for non-circular sliding surfaces.
sections.applicability: Worked example of stability checks for a mass mixed embankment foundation.

sections.title: Step 7
sections.summary: Example Step 7: with the settlement and stability criteria satisfied, prepare the plans and specifications for procurement and construction of the mass mixed embankment foundation, specifying the required unconfined compressive strength rather than a binder factor (p. 7-33).
sections.body: Prepare the plans and specifications for procurement and construction (p. 7-33). As noted in Step 3 of the example, the specifications are written around the required unconfined compressive strength and do not require any particular binder factor.

Specify required UCS, not binder factor.

sections.title: Construction Specifications and Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Container section on mass mixing specifications and QA: specification development with an outline of section headings, quality assurance alternatives to coring for weak soil-cement, and instrumentation, monitoring and construction control (pp. 7-36 to 7-39).
sections.body: This section covers specification development (3.4.1), a summary of quality assurance (3.4.2), and a summary of instrumentation, monitoring and construction control (3.4.3) for mass mixing, pp. 7-36 to 7-39.
sections.applicability: Mass mixing (shallow soil mixing and mass stabilization) of soft ground at 100% or nearly 100% coverage in transportation projects.

sections.title: Specification Development
sections.summary: Mass mixing example specifications are at GeoTechTools and must be carefully edited; like deep mixing they are end-result specifications. Gives an outline: General (scope, references, qualifications, submittals), Materials and Equipment, Execution (mix design, demonstration, production, QC/QA, acceptance, remediation), Measurement and Payment (pp. 7-36 to 7-38).
sections.body: Example specifications are available at GeoTechTools; any adapted from other mass mixing projects should be very carefully reviewed and edited (p. 7-36). Like deep mixing, mass mixing uses end-result specifications because of substantial differences in contractor equipment and procedures. A mass mixing specification may include: 1. General (scope, project objectives and site conditions; references; qualifications of contractor project and personnel experience; submittals of qualifications, equipment, materials, laboratory mix design report, field demonstration section plan and report, work plan, QC/QA plan, daily reports and summary report); 2. Materials and Equipment; 3. Execution (laboratory mix design program; field demonstration section; production mixing; QC and QA of materials, equipment, geometry, mixing process, sampling and testing, in situ testing and field load testing; acceptance criteria for geometry, consistency of process control and unconfined compressive strength; remedial work); and 4. Measurement and Payment (mobilization, laboratory mix design testing and field demonstration program as lump sums; mixing including QC/QA measurements, testing and documentation as a price per cubic yard) (pp. 7-36 to 7-38).
key_points: End-result specifications for mass mixing.
Acceptance criteria: geometry, consistency of process control, unconfined compressive strength.
Payment: lump sums for mobilization, mix design and demonstration; mixing per cubic yard.
sections.applicability: Drafting a mass mixing specification.

sections.title: Summary of Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Mass mixing QA is like deep mixing except for weak soil-cement: core is hard to recover below 100 psi UCS (done as low as 50 psi), so wet grab sampling, cone or blade penetrometers, and full-scale embankment load tests are used; lower variability factors or higher FS may be warranted (pp. 7-38 to 7-39).
sections.body: QA for mass mixing is similar to deep mixing except for coring and testing when the soil-cement strength is low (p. 7-38). Coring has succeeded on projects specifying UCS as low as 50 psi, but core is generally hard to recover for soil-cement under 100 psi, particularly if strength is variable and the material contains clumps of unmixed soil at the scale of the core diameter. Other QA methods are therefore often used: wet grab sampling right after mixing when the mixture is fluid enough, using a bucket with a door or flap, with specimens formed in molds like concrete cylinders and tested in unconfined compression; cone penetrometers where the soil-cement is not too strong, or for very low strengths the blade penetrometer test developed for dry-method deep-mixed columns, whose welded blade tests more material and gives less erratic results; and full-scale embankment load tests monitored with settlement plates and inclinometer casings. Coring remains preferred but is impractical for weak soil-cement. Because QC/QA is typically less thorough than for deep mixing, somewhat lower variability factors and/or larger factors of safety may be warranted, judged case by case; the design example applied a lower variability factor than a deep mixing project with good QC/QA would normally use (p. 7-39).
key_points: Core recovery difficult below about 100 psi UCS; coring achieved as low as 50 psi.
Alternatives: wet grab samples, cone or blade penetrometers, full-scale embankment load tests.
Lower variability factors and/or larger FS may be warranted for mass mixing.
sections.applicability: Quality assurance of low-strength mass mixed soil-cement.

sections.title: Summary of Instrumentation, Monitoring, and Construction Control
sections.summary: Instrumentation, monitoring and construction control for shallow soil mixing are similar to vertical-axis deep mixing; for mass stabilization with an excavator-mounted drum, geometry and thoroughness are operator dependent, so close QC and QA observation is essential (p. 7-39).
sections.body: Instrumentation, monitoring and construction control for shallow soil mixing are similar to the corresponding equipment and processes for deep mixing with vertical-axis mixing equipment (p. 7-39). For mass stabilization with a horizontal-axis mixing drum mounted on an excavator, mixing geometry and thoroughness are operator dependent, and close observation of construction by QC and QA personnel is essential.
key_points: Shallow soil mixing: monitored like vertical-axis deep mixing.
Mass stabilization: operator dependent; close QC/QA observation essential.
sections.applicability: Mass mixing (shallow soil mixing and mass stabilization) of soft ground at 100% or nearly 100% coverage in transportation projects.

sections.title: Cost Data
sections.summary: The factors that influence the cost of mass mixing are similar to those that influence the cost of deep mixing, such as treatment volume, depth, specified strength, soil types, binder availability, site access and QC/QA requirements (p. 7-39).
sections.body: The factors that influence the cost of mass mixing are similar to those that influence the cost of deep mixing (p. 7-39), listed in Section 2.5. Cost components are given in Section 3.5.1.
key_points: Same cost factors as deep mixing.
sections.applicability: Mass mixing (shallow soil mixing and mass stabilization) of soft ground at 100% or nearly 100% coverage in transportation projects.

sections.title: Cost Components
sections.summary: Mass mixing mobilization costs can be $25,000 to $150,000 including support equipment; unit costs $15 to $75 per cubic yard, lower on large projects in competitive markets; the same factors and qualifications as for deep mixing cost estimates apply (p. 7-39).
sections.body: Mobilization costs for mass mixing can be in the range of $25,000 to $150,000, including support equipment (p. 7-39). Unit costs can be in the range of $15 to $75 per cubic yard, with lower costs associated with large projects in competitive markets. The same types of factors and qualifications used for estimating deep mixing costs also apply to mass mixing costs.
key_points: Mobilization: $25,000 to $150,000.
Unit cost: $15 to $75 per cubic yard.

sections.title: Case History
sections.summary: Case history (Gamin and Mann 2010): dry-method mass stabilization at 100% coverage of about 12 ft of very soft organic silt under MSE-wall approaches and a bridge founded on MSE fill; design shear strength 2,160 psf; 5 ft x 20 ft cells; blade penetrometer QC at one test per 2,500 sq ft (pp. 7-39 to 7-40).
sections.body: A two-lane, four-span, 218-foot-long bridge was built over a discharge canal to improve truck access (Gamin and Mann 2010). Approach embankments are supported by MSE walls and the bridge is founded directly on the MSE wall fill. Criteria: total and differential settlements limited to 1 inch and 0.5 inch, and factors of safety for overall stability and MSE wall bearing capacity at least 2 and 3 (p. 7-39). The subsurface was several feet of sand over very soft organic silt averaging 12 feet thick, over limestone or dense cemented sand. Dry-method mass mixing stabilized the organic silt at 100% coverage, extending 5 feet beyond the MSE wall footings; a design shear strength of 2,160 psf satisfied the criteria. A laboratory mix design program with Portland cement set the target binder weight per unit volume (p. 7-40). The upper sand was stripped and stockpiled; an excavator-mounted horizontal-axis tool blended dry binder into the silt in adjacent cells about 5 feet by 20 feet; a geotextile and the sand were then placed as surcharge during curing. QC controlled binder dose and mixing energy, with logs of cell, target and actual binder and total mixing time. QA used the blade penetrometer test at a minimum of one test per 2,500 square feet, supplemented by SPT borings and coring; with a relatively high binder factor, tests were done one to four days after mixing and cells lacking strength were re-mixed. Petroleum-contaminated soil was encountered; because the dry method produces no spoils and cement stabilizes petroleum contamination, no additional work was needed.
key_points: Criteria: total settlement 1 inch, differential 0.5 inch; FS overall 2, bearing 3.
Organic silt averaging 12 ft thick treated at 100% coverage, 5 ft beyond MSE wall footings.
Design shear strength of soil-cement 2,160 psf; Portland cement binder.
Cells about 5 ft by 20 ft; blade penetrometer at least one test per 2,500 sq ft, 1 to 4 days after mixing.
Dry method produced no spoils; contaminated soil stabilized without extra work.
